samples.summary: HMAC-"signed" double submit adds no defence against the cookie-planting attacker it is documented to stop; outside NODE_ENV=production the forced-login CSRF (and the CLI browser-binding) is still fully open
samples.evidence:
`stateSignature()` (github-auth.guard.ts:108) computes `state = w.HMAC(JWT_SECRET, cookieValue)` and the comment at lines 100-107 claims "the attacker can plant a cookie but cannot produce the `state` that matches it, so the forced-login CSRF stays shut even where the prefix cannot be used" (repeated in docs/design/backend.md and rest-api.md).

That is false. The cookie value is server-generated and returned to the requester: a single unauthenticated `curl -i https://backend/auth/github` yields both halves of a *valid* pair — `Set-Cookie: wafflebase_oauth_state=C` and `Location: https://github.com/...&state=w.HMAC(C)` (guard lines 249-255 mint both on the same response). An attacker who can plant a cookie for the registrable domain therefore plants exactly that `C` and replays the matching signature; the HMAC buys nothing over a plain double submit. The only control that actually resists cookie planting is the `__Host-` prefix, and `secureCookies()` (line 44-46) turns it off — along with `Secure` — for every deployment that does not set `NODE_ENV=production` (self-hosted docker/compose behind TLS is the common case). In such a deployment a sibling-subdomain XSS/takeover or an http `Set-Cookie` injection re-opens the forced-login CSRF this change exists to close.

The CLI half is weaker still: `StateEntry.browserBinding` is stored and compared as the raw cookie value (auth.controller.ts:294-299), so the same cookie planter — who mints the CLI state token themselves and so already knows it — completes the CLI forced-login and captures an authorization code for the victim's account at their own loopback port, which the risk table in docs/design/rest-api.md asserts is prevented.

A state that is bound to something the attacker cannot obtain (e.g. HMAC over cookie value *plus* a per-login server secret the attacker never receives, or a server-side entry keyed by the cookie) is what the comment describes; this implementation is not it. At minimum the security claim in the comment and both design docs should be corrected so operators do not mis-assess a non-production deployment.

samples.summary: New access-log redaction misses the share-link credential when it rides in the path: `GET /share-links/:token/resolve` is logged verbatim
samples.evidence:
`logSafeUrl` only ever touches the query string — `const query = url.indexOf('?'); if (query === -1) return url;` (log-safe-url.ts:102-103) — and `SENSITIVE_PARAMS` is keyed on parameter *names*. The share-link token is documented (and treated in this diff) as "the whole of that document's access control", and it is carried in two shapes:
- `GET /documents/:id/file?token=<t>` (document-file.controller.ts:40) — covered by the new `token` entry;
- `GET /share-links/:token/resolve` (share-link.controller.ts:67-68, unauthenticated, resolves documentId/role/title for the bearer) — the same credential as a *path segment*, which `logSafeUrl` returns untouched.

So the live token lands in the access-log `url` field in full. `customLogLevel` (app.module.ts:49-61) puts any 4xx/5xx on that route at `warn`/`error`, so it survives the default `info` level (and every request survives when `LOG_LEVEL=debug`, which is normal in staging) — exactly the "replayable credential parked in a file operators, log shippers and agent harnesses all read" that the new control was added to prevent. The redaction reads as covering the share credential (its own doc comment names it) while covering only one of its two carriers.

Searched: grep for `@Query('...')`/`@Param(` across packages/backend/src to enumerate credential-bearing routes; read share-link.controller.ts and document-file.controller.ts; read log-safe-url.ts and its spec — no path-segment redaction exists anywhere.
searchedFor: grep req.url|originalUrl across packages/backend/src for other URL log sites

samples.summary: The JWT signing key is reused as an HMAC key over fully client-controlled input (the presented state cookie), violating key separation
samples.evidence:
`bindingSecret()` returns `JWT_SECRET` — the same key `AuthService`/`JwtStrategy` use to sign and verify HS256 session, refresh and Yorkie tokens (auth.service.ts:51, jwt.strategy.ts:18) — and it is fed to `createHmac('sha256', secret).update(cookieValue)` (github-auth.guard.ts:108). On the callback path the message is attacker-chosen: `verifyCallbackState` computes `stateSignature(bindingSecret(...), cookie)` over whatever value the client sends in the `wafflebase_oauth_state` cookie (auth.controller.ts:279-282). HS256 JWT signing is the same primitive over the same key, so this is a chosen-message HMAC operation with the JWT key.

Today the computed value is only compared, never returned or logged, so it is not yet a forgery oracle — but nothing in the code marks that as load-bearing, and a future debug log/error message that echoes `expected` would hand an attacker `HMAC(JWT_SECRET, <chosen header.payload>)`, i.e. a forged session token. Derive a separate subkey (e.g. `HKDF`/`HMAC(JWT_SECRET, 'oauth-state')`) rather than using the signing key directly.

samples.summary: Unauthenticated, unthrottled `/auth/github?mode=cli` lets any client insert unbounded 5-minute entries into the in-memory state map, with an O(n) sweep per insert
samples.evidence: `GET /auth/github` carries no `@Throttle` (auth.controller.ts:110-112), unlike `/auth/github/callback` and `/auth/cli/exchange`. The consent gate is a double submit the *client itself* supplies both halves of — `hasConfirmation` compares `?cli_confirm=X` against the request's own `Cookie: wafflebase_cli_confirm=X` (github-auth.guard.ts:261-272) — so a non-browser attacker satisfies it with one curl flag and reaches `createState()` (line 238) on every request. Each call adds a `StateEntry` held for 5 minutes and then runs `cleanup()`, which iterates the whole map (cli-auth.store.ts:141-145), so cost grows quadratically with the flood. A sustained unauthenticated request stream therefore drives both memory and CPU on a public endpoint. (The browser branch is stateless, and the pre-change code had the same unthrottled `createState`, so this is amplified rather than introduced — but the new O(n) sweep per insert and the extra round trip make it worth a cap or a throttle.)

samples.summary: The CLI consent interstitial — the change's only human-in-the-loop gate — is served with no `X-Frame-Options` / CSP `frame-ancestors`, so clickjacking is the natural bypass
samples.evidence:
`res.type('html').send(this.renderCliConsent(...))` (auth.controller.ts:121-125) sets no framing headers, and I found no helmet/CSP middleware in main.ts. The whole gate is one click on `<a class="continue" href=...>`, which is precisely the interaction clickjacking targets: frame the page invisibly over a decoy and harvest the click that authorises a code delivery to `port=<attacker's listener>`.

In a current browser the attack is blocked incidentally rather than deliberately: the confirm cookie is `SameSite=Lax` (loginCookieOptions, github-auth.guard.ts:68-75), so the in-frame link navigation is not top-level and the cookie is withheld, and the re-render's `Set-Cookie` is refused in a third-party context. That is a fragile reason for a security gate to hold; `X-Frame-Options: DENY` (or `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'`) on this response states the intent.

Searched: read packages/backend/src/main.ts (no helmet/CSP), grep for helmet/frame-ancestors/X-Frame-Options in packages/backend/src — none found.
searchedFor: read packages/backend/src/main.ts for helmet / security headers

samples.summary: Consent page's continue link is built from `req.path` and HTML-escaped but never validated as a same-origin absolute path
samples.evidence: `const href = escapeHtml(`${self}?${params.toString()}`)` where `self = req.path` (auth.controller.ts:125, 152). `escapeHtml` neutralises HTML metacharacters but not URL semantics: a `req.path` beginning with `//` would render a protocol-relative link, sending the confirm token, nonce and PKCE challenge to an off-site host on the user's click. I could not construct a reachable case — Express 5's router will not match `//auth/github` against the `/auth/github` route, so `req.path` should always start with a case-variant of `/auth/github` — hence low confidence. Cheap to close: assert `self.startsWith('/') && !self.startsWith('//')` or just rebuild the link from a constant route literal.

verdict.reason: Every claim in the finding is present as described. stateSignature() is a bare HMAC over the cookie value only (github-auth.guard.ts:108-110), and canActivate mints the cookie (issueLoginCookie at :250, res.cookie at :291) and the matching state (:251-254) on the SAME unauthenticated response, which GitHubStrategy.authenticate forwards to GitHub as `state` (github.strategy.ts:61-68) and thus into the Location header. So any requester can obtain a valid (cookieValue, w.HMAC(cookieValue)) pair with one curl, meaning the signature provides no defence over a plain double submit against an attacker who can plant a cookie — contradicting the comment at github-auth.guard.ts:100-107 and the same claim in docs/design/backend.md:110-112 and :352-355. The only control that does resist cookie planting, the __Host- prefix (and Secure), is disabled for every deployment not setting NODE_ENV=production (github-auth.guard.ts:44-46, :60, :71); grep confirms this is the sole definition with no override. The callback path is stateless and recomputes the signature from whatever cookie is presented (auth.controller.ts:273-288), so no other guard closes the gap. The CLI half compares browserBinding as the raw cookie value (guard:241, auth.controller.ts:293-299) and the consent gate is a raw cookie/param equality (guard:265-271), so the same cookie planter completes the CLI forced-login and captures a code at their own loopback port — the exact attack the risk table at docs/design/rest-api.md:399 asserts is prevented. This is in the security lane (weakened auth/CSRF binding, ineffective cryptographic check, security documentation that would cause operators to mis-assess a non-production/self-hosted TLS deployment) and is a real major weakness, not refutable as not-present, already-guarded, or out-of-scope.

verdict.reason: Verified in the repo, no counterexample exists. `logSafeUrl` (packages/backend/src/logging/log-safe-url.ts:100-113) returns the URL verbatim when there is no query string and otherwise only rewrites query parameters by name (SENSITIVE_PARAMS, :35-55); no code path inspects path segments. The share-link bearer token is carried as a path segment on the unauthenticated `@Get('share-links/:token/resolve')` route (share-link.controller.ts:67-76), and `findByToken` (share-link.service.ts:102-117) grants documentId/role/title on token possession alone, so it is a live replayable credential. The only logger wiring is app.module.ts:30-93, where the req serializer emits `url: logSafeUrl(req.url)` (:70) and pino's `redact.paths` (:78-85) covers only authorization/cookie/set-cookie headers — never `req.url` — so there is no second layer. `customLogLevel` (:49-61) puts 4xx at `warn` and 5xx/err at `error` (surviving the default `info` level), and `level: process.env.LOG_LEVEL ?? 'info'` (:32) means every resolve, including successful ones with a valid token, is logged under `LOG_LEVEL=debug`. main.ts has no middleware that rewrites req.url before logging (:48-64). Repo-wide grep for logSafe|safeUrl|sanitizeUrl|scrubUrl|maskUrl|redactPath|log-safe found only this module, its spec, app.module.ts, unrelated frontend/core URL-detection files, and the agent-harness `redactSecrets` (which does not touch the backend access log); grep for redact|serializers|customLogLevel|LoggerModule across packages/backend shows exactly one logger config. The spec itself asserts pass-through for query-less URLs (log-safe-url.spec.ts:69-70), confirming the gap by test. Sensitive-data exposure in logs is in the security lane; the control reads as covering the share credential (its doc comment at :28-33 names it) while covering only one of its two carriers.
